off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R"),
                       O("H", "WR", -1.5, 10.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.5, "Z"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X")]
dfn = over_front(+1) + [D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 16.5, "CB"), D("SS", "S", 12.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 12.0, -7.0, "FS"),
                        D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -16.0, "CB")]   # X and his cornerback: outside the drawn window
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6, title="Drill 2: base 4-3 against three receivers")
p.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-9.4, 18.8), window=(-7.6, 13.6))
say(f, p, 2.6, 10.5, "nobody over him", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 2: 11 personnel, shotgun, tight end and two receivers on the right (H in the slot, Z wide; X wide left, outside the picture). The defense is in its base 4-3, set as an Over to the tight end, with two deep safeties. The Sam (ringed) is still at his base spot outside the tight end; nobody is over the slot receiver.](05-02-even-fronts_files/figure-html/fig-drill-2-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-2}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The Sam has to choose, and every choice costs something, which is the point of the formation.**

- **If the Sam stays in the box**, the defense has seven against the run (four linemen and three linebackers)
  but nobody near the slot receiver. A quick throw to H, a hitch, a bubble screen or a quick out, gets an easy
  five or six yards on second-and-6.
- **If the Sam walks out over the slot** (to an apex, halfway between the tight end and H), the throw is
  covered, at least by a linebacker. But now the box has six defenders (four linemen, the Mike and the Will)
  against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), with two safeties twelve yards deep. That's a light
  box, and the offense will happily run the ball. Worse, the Over's bubble is still there: the weak guard is
  free to climb to the Will.
- **If the defense rotates** instead, the strong safety buzzes down over the slot (or into the box), the Sam
  stays, and the free safety moves to the middle: a one-high shell, the move Seattle's defenses made a
  habit of (see the nickel section). Now the box and the slot are both covered, but one safety guards the
  whole deep middle against three receivers who can all run vertical routes, so the offense's answer is
  [four verticals](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-verticals), or a seam route, over the top.

Every answer gives something up. This is why defenses substitute a nickel back against 11 personnel, and why offenses that keep a fullback or a
second tight end on the field until the defense commits to base personnel can then spread out without
substituting and force exactly this choice. The quarterback's pre-snap read is simple: count the box, look at the
slot, and throw or hand off accordingly, the logic of the [RPO](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. Run against the wide-9.** First-and-10, a shotgun one-back set with the tight end on the right.
Both defensive ends are in wide-9 alignments, the tackles in a 3 (right) and a 1 (left), with the Sam standing
off the ball outside the tight end. Where is the offense's best run, and which defender decides whether it
works?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-3 .cell execution_count=15}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -2.0, "R")]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -(4.8 + 2.3), "w9"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", -1), "1"),
       D("DT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("wide9", 1), "w9"),
       D("WILL", "LB", 4.8, -2.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.8, 0.7, "M"), D("SAM", "LB", 4.6, 6.0, "S")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10, title="Drill 3: two wide-9 ends")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-10.6, 10.6), window=(-7.6, 7.6))
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Drill 3: both ends in wide-9 alignments, in sprinter's stances; a 3-technique on the right guard and a 1 on the center's left shoulder; three linebackers, the Sam off the ball outside the tight end.](05-02-even-fronts_files/figure-html/fig-drill-3-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-3}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Off tackle, inside either end, and the linebacker on that side decides it.** This front has two big lanes,
and the drill has more than one good answer.

- **Toward the tight end**, the lane between the 3-technique and the right end spans two gaps, the C and the
  D, and the wide-9's whole job on the snap is to go upfield, not to close it. Against this front the right
  tackle and the tight end are *both* uncovered, so the blocking is clean: the right guard takes the 3, the
  right tackle climbs to the Mike, the tight end blocks the Sam, and the end is left alone to run himself out
  of the play. The Sam is the only defender who owns that lane, so he has to fill it before the back gets
  there, ideally meeting the tight end at the line so the back has to cut back inside. If he's late, the next
  defender is a safety ten yards downfield.
- **Away from the tight end**, the lane between the 1 and the left end is even wider on paper, and it sits on
  the bubble: the left guard is uncovered. The center and left guard double the 1 and one climbs, the left
  tackle climbs to the Will, and again the end is left alone. Here the Will decides, with the same two-gap
  problem and a 300-pound tackle coming at him.

Many coaches would still go strong first, because the tight end gives them an extra blocker on that side
and a running back can bounce outside him if the Sam over-fills. Either way, the end can help by *squeezing* when he
reads run, closing down the line behind the play rather than rushing past it, and the defense's real answer
is a safety who arrives in time. That is the trade from @fig-wide-nine-front, live: the ends' rush is a bet
that the linebackers and safeties will be on time.

The best modern answer of all uses the end's alignment against him. A shotgun offense can run inside zone,
leave the backside wide-9 unblocked and *read* him: if he chases the back, the quarterback keeps the ball and
runs where the end used to be. That is the [zone read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-read) of
[Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd), and its pass-game cousin, the
[RPO](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd), punishes the same man the same way.
:::
:::

## Back to the huddle

The chapter opened with a defensive tackle jogging across the center when the tight end lined up on the
right, a linebacker walking up onto the line outside the tight end, and, two plays later, the same defense
staying put. Now you can read it. The tackle over the right guard was only standing there while the offense
huddled: until the tight end shows his side, the defense doesn't know where its front goes. On the first
play the call was a **4-3 Under**: once the tight end set up on the right, the 3-technique went to the weak
guard, away from him, and the Sam walked up to make the strong-side edge two men deep at the line. On the
second, with the tight end on the left, the call was an **Over**: the tackle was already on the guard on the
tight end's side, so nobody had to cross, and the Sam stayed off the ball. One word, and the formation, set eleven alignments. And each was a bet about which
guard to leave free and where the run would be met.

## Takeaways

- **An even front sets its linemen in pairs, with nobody head-up on the center.** Two tackles can't cover
  three interior linemen, so the center or a guard is always free; every even front is a decision about
  which one, and which linebacker answers for him.
- **Over and Under are the same players, leaning opposite ways from a strength call.** The Over puts the
  3-technique and its linemen toward the tight end and leaves the weak guard uncovered for the Will; the Under
  sends the 3-technique to the weak side to rush one-on-one, puts the Sam on the line to harden the strong-side
  edge, and leaves the strong guard uncovered under the Mike. Runs aim at the uncovered guard: the bubble.
- **Strength is relative, so offenses move it.** A tight-end shift can make half a front re-set in a second
  and a half, or the defense can check Over to Under and move only the linebackers, because an Over one way
  is the same line as an Under the other way. Every answer gives something up.
- **The wide-9 buys pass rush with run lanes.** Unblocked at the snap, the ends reach full speed before the
  tackle can touch them, and the two-gap lanes inside them become the linebackers' and safeties' problem. With a stout interior and fast linebackers
  (the 2017 Eagles) it can stop the run; without them it gets run through.
- **The bear front covers the center and both guards, and the 46 built a defense on it.** With no uncovered
  interior lineman, double teams, climbing guards and pullers all become hard. Buddy Ryan's 1985 Bears
  smothered two-back offenses with it; three receivers and quick throws made it a situational front, now
  used near the goal line and against zone-running teams.
- **Against 11 personnel the line stays and the Sam goes.** The four linemen keep their rule; the third
  linebacker becomes a nickel back, and someone, often a safety, takes his job on the tight end.
